title: Sends Troops to Border for Migrant Caravan
description_medium: On October 29, 2018, the Pentagon announced that it would send 5,200 active-duty troops to the southwestern border as two migrant caravans moved through Mexico. The deployment, dubbed Operation Faithful Patriot, followed Trump’s calls for military involvement and a Homeland Security request for support. Commanders said troops would assist Customs and Border Protection rather than perform law-enforcement duties.
description_long: The Pentagon announced on October 29, 2018, that 5,200 active-duty service members would deploy to the U.S.-Mexico border under Operation Faithful Patriot. The move followed President Donald Trump’s public demands for military involvement as two caravans of Central American migrants traveled through Mexico toward the United States. Customs and Border Protection said it was adding 1,000 officers and sought Defense Department support; officials described one caravan as about 3,500 people and another as roughly 3,000. The forces were assigned to Texas, Arizona and California. Their work included reinforcing ports of entry, building barriers and temporary facilities, medical support, and helicopter transport for CBP personnel. Military commanders said troops would support the civilian agency and would not conduct arrests or other law enforcement, which federal law bars active-duty forces from doing domestically. Officials initially described a 45-day mission. The deployment drew attention because it was ordered in the closing week before the 2018 midterm elections, while Trump was campaigning on border security and describing the caravan as a threat. The documented order is a military support deployment, not a transfer of immigration enforcement authority to the armed forces.
source_access_notes: The linked Washington Post article was inaccessible; ABC News and an AP-carried CBS report covered the same October 29 deployment.
rationale: The event is the 5,200-person deployment order. ABC and AP report the operational purpose and legal limit on troops; this preserves the distinction between military support and civilian law enforcement.

title: Invokes Emergency Authority to Expedite Arms Transfers to Saudi Arabia, UAE, and Jordan
description_medium: On May 24, 2019, the Trump administration invoked an emergency under the Arms Export Control Act to move forward with 22 arms-transfer cases worth about $8.1 billion for Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Jordan. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo cited tensions with Iran. Congress had held many of the cases amid concern over the Yemen war and Saudi human-rights abuses.
description_long: On May 24, 2019, Secretary of State Mike Pompeo invoked emergency authority under the Arms Export Control Act to waive the usual congressional review period for 22 arms-transfer cases involving Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Jordan. The transfers were valued at approximately $8.1 billion and included precision-guided munitions, aircraft support and other military equipment. Pompeo cited Iranian threats and said the sales would help regional partners deter aggression. The action overrode congressional holds on 15 of the 22 cases, some of which lawmakers had blocked for more than a year. Members of Congress had raised concerns about civilian casualties in Yemen from the Saudi-led coalition and the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi. The decision intensified an existing dispute over Congress’s role in reviewing weapons sales and U.S. support for the Yemen campaign. A State Department inspector general later found that the emergency certification met the statute’s procedural requirements, while also concluding that the department had not fully assessed or mitigated civilian-casualty risks associated with some transfers. The OIG did not assess whether Iran-related threats legally constituted an emergency. The event was the waiver and notification that let the pending cases proceed; it did not itself establish that every listed item was immediately delivered or used.

title.original: Approves Emergency Arms Sales to Saudi and UAE
title.corrected: Invokes Emergency Authority to Expedite Arms Transfers to Saudi Arabia, UAE, and Jordan
title.reason: The administration waived the statutory review period for 22 cases; Jordan was also included, and the event was the emergency certification that allowed them to proceed.

source_access_notes: The linked IranWatch and archived State Department pages were inaccessible. Used Reuters syndication and the State Department OIG review of the same May 2019 emergency action.
rationale: The action covered Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Jordan; Congress had placed holds on 15 cases. Later OIG review found procedural compliance alongside incomplete assessment of civilian-harm risks.

title: Announces Planned End of Honduras Temporary Protected Status
description_medium: On May 4, 2018, Homeland Security Secretary Kirstjen Nielsen announced that the government would end Temporary Protected Status for Hondurans, with termination scheduled for January 5, 2020. DHS said conditions had improved since Hurricane Mitch, which led to the designation in 1999. More than 50,000 Hondurans had been protected from removal and could work legally under TPS.
description_long: Homeland Security Secretary Kirstjen Nielsen announced on May 4, 2018, that the United States would terminate Temporary Protected Status for Honduras. The designation had followed Hurricane Mitch, which devastated the country in 1998; DHS said the disruption in living conditions had decreased enough that it no longer met the statutory basis for protection. The department set January 5, 2020, as the termination date, an 18-month transition intended to give beneficiaries time to prepare and Honduras time to plan for returning citizens. TPS allowed eligible Hondurans already in the United States to remain temporarily and obtain work authorization, but did not itself provide permanent residence. Axios reported that more than 50,000 people were affected. The announcement formed part of the administration’s broader effort to end several long-running TPS designations. Its planned deadline did not unfold as announced: litigation over the terminations led DHS in 2019 to say it would not implement or enforce the Honduras decision while the case was pending, and a later administration formally rescinded the termination. Thus the event was the 2018 decision and proposed wind-down, not an immediate loss of protected status for beneficiaries.

title.corrected: Announces Planned End of Honduras Temporary Protected Status
title.reason: DHS announced a future termination date; the status did not end on the announcement date and the decision was later stayed and rescinded.

source_access_notes: The DHS release URL was inaccessible. Read Axios coverage, the 2018 Federal Register notice, and the 2019 Federal Register notice documenting that DHS would not enforce the termination pending litigation.
rationale: The 2018 notice set a future end date and described the hurricane-based rationale; the 2019 notice is needed to distinguish announcement from implementation.

title: Signs Asylum Cooperative Agreement with Honduras
description_medium: The United States and Honduras signed an Asylum Cooperative Agreement in New York on September 25, 2019. It created a framework for transferring some people who sought protection at the U.S. border to Honduras to pursue claims there. The agreement excluded Honduran nationals and included exceptions for certain people, including unaccompanied minors. It entered into force in March 2020.
description_long: The United States and Honduras signed an Asylum Cooperative Agreement in New York on September 25, 2019. The treaty established a process under which the United States could refer some people who sought protection at the U.S. border to Honduras for a Honduran protection determination. It did not apply to Honduran nationals or habitual residents, and the agreement left responsibility with the United States for unaccompanied minors and some people who entered with valid visas or did not need visas. Honduras agreed not to remove a referred claimant to another country before a final decision on that claim, and the two governments committed to develop procedures governing transfers and the system’s capacity. The agreement entered into force on March 25, 2020, after the required implementation plan was established; signing it in 2019 did not mean transfers began that day. The agreement was part of the Trump administration’s effort to make some asylum seekers pursue protection in another country rather than have every claim adjudicated in the United States. Its text framed the process as burden-sharing and reaffirmed non-refoulement obligations, while requiring the governments to plan for transfer procedures, volumes, and Honduras’s institutional capacity. The event is the signing of the bilateral framework, distinct from its later entry into force and implementation.
source_access_notes: The linked DHS announcement was inaccessible. Read the signed agreement preserved by the Government Publishing Office and same-day CBS reporting.
rationale: The agreement’s text defines covered claimants, exceptions and the entry-into-force date; these details clarify that signing did not itself initiate transfers.

title: Announces Temporary Hold on U.S. Funding to the WHO
description_medium: On April 14, 2020, President Donald Trump announced a 60- to 90-day hold on U.S. funding to the World Health Organization while his administration reviewed its response to COVID-19. Trump accused the WHO of mismanaging and concealing the outbreak, claims he presented as the reason for the review. The United States was the WHO’s largest government contributor.
description_long: At a White House briefing on April 14, 2020, President Donald Trump announced that the United States would pause funding to the World Health Organization for 60 to 90 days while his administration reviewed the agency’s handling of the COVID-19 pandemic. Trump accused the WHO of mismanaging the outbreak and failing to share information quickly, and said the pause would allow the government to assess the organization’s role. Those were the president’s allegations, not findings established by the funding announcement. The decision came as the WHO coordinated international public-health guidance and response activity. The Congressional Research Service reported that the United States was the largest government contributor, providing 22 percent of the WHO’s assessed core budget, and also made substantial voluntary contributions for health programs. Members of Congress disagreed about the pause: some supported Trump’s criticism, while others urged continued support for the WHO’s pandemic work. The announcement left open which categories of funding would be withheld and how the administration would carry out the hold. The event was the announced review and temporary funding pause, not a formal U.S. withdrawal from the organization or proof that all American support had stopped immediately.

title.original: Halts U.S. Funding to the WHO
title.corrected: Announces Temporary Hold on U.S. Funding to the WHO
title.reason: The April 14 event was an announcement of a 60–90-day hold pending review; the source did not establish that all funding had already stopped.

source_access_notes: The supplied Wikipedia URL was unrelated and the White House transcript was not accessible. Used Axios’s same-day report and the Congressional Research Service’s funding overview.
rationale: The event was an announced, time-limited review and hold. CRS provides the funding context, while Axios records the president’s stated allegations and the open implementation questions.
